<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-adapted cases and handled the Pressure Questions format correctly, but A controlled the debate's central frame more effectively. A's "reach vs. miss" framing forced B's supposedly targeted fix (community eligibility / data matching) into an admission that it is itself a form of universalism at the building level, and B never fully closed the resulting "sliver" gap, explicitly conceding it as "a real design problem" — a concession A exploited decisively in closing. A also raised an administrative-cost point (a two-tier system still needs account tracking and a cashier-visible seam) that B's rebuttals never directly answered. B's strongest counter — that universal spending dilutes a fixed food budget and that A's political-durability argument secretly concedes the comparison is about program safety rather than reach — was sharp and forced A onto weaker ground for a round, but A recovered by reasserting the reach argument ("she eats") and pointing out B never named a redirection mechanism for "saved" dollars, a pressure question B's answer sidestepped rather than met. The debate was close and both sides argued with discipline and plausible grounding, but A ended with the cleaner, more memorable resolution of the central clash.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's turn of B's own community-eligibility proposal ([A2.1]-[A2.4]) into a concession that stigma-elimination requires abandoning individual means testing, combined with B's later explicit concession in [B4.2] that the residual "sliver" is "a real design problem" — which A converted into the decisive moral frame in closing.</best_rebuttal>
